```{r Visual-scheme, include=FALSE}
#Reusable graph theme https://rfortherestofus.com/2025/04/ggplot2-theme

theme_mygraphs <- function(base_size = 12,
                           base_family = "Arial") {

  theme_minimal(
    base_size = base_size,
    base_family = base_family
  ) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        size = 15,
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222",
        hjust = 0.5,
        margin = margin(b = 10)
      ),

      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        size = 11,
        color = "#555555",
        hjust = 0.5
      ),

      axis.title = element_text(
        size = 11,
        face = "bold",
        color = "#222222"
      ),

      axis.text = element_text(
        size = 10,
        color = "#333333"
      ),

         # Spacing
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 12, 10, 12
                           ),   
      
      # Gridlines
      panel.grid.major = element_line(
        color = "#E8E8E8",
        linewidth = 0.4
      ),

      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

      # Legends
      legend.position = "bottom",

      legend.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        size = 10
      ),

      legend.text = element_text(
        size = 10
      ),

      legend.background = element_blank()
      )
}
```

## Clean Data (create columns that will be used for our analysis)
```{r 24-hr-column}
# Add 24-hour time column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp = mdy_hms(transit_timestamp),
    hour = hour(timestamp)
  )
```

```{r Day-categories}
# Add categories for morning, afternoon, evening, night
# Morning (5am - 10:59am), afternoon (11am - 3:59pm), evening (4pm - 8:59pm), night (9pm - 4:59am)
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    time_of_day = case_when(
      hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning",
      hour >= 11 & hour < 16 ~ "Mid Day",
      hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening",
      TRUE ~ "Night"
    )
  )

```

```{r Day-of-week column}
# Add day of week column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    day_of_week = wday(timestamp, label = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r Weekend-weekday column}
# Weekend vs. Weekday column
project <- project %>%
  mutate(day_type = if_else(day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun"), "Weekend", "Weekday"))
```

```{r More Cleaning}
project$time_of_day <- as.factor(project$time_of_day)
project$day_of_week <- as.factor(project$day_of_week)
project$day_type <- as.factor(project$day_type)
```

```{r Commute Type column}
# Suggestion commuter hours 
project <- project %>%
  mutate(
    commute_type = case_when(
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 5 & hour < 11 ~ "Morning Commute",
      day_type == "Weekday" & hour >= 16 & hour < 21 ~ "Evening Commute",
      TRUE ~ "Other Hours"
    )
  )

```

## Hypothesis Testing
Questions of interest:

- “How do NYC subway ridership volumes vary throughout the day during the week of September 15-21, 2024?” -- Anova and post hoc

- Which hours have the highest ridership average (weekdays vs. weekends)? 

- Do these hours correspond to commuting periods? 
  
**T-Tests: Commute vs. Non-commute; Weekday vs. Weekend**
```{r}
hourly_ridership <- project %>%
  mutate(commute_period = if_else(commute_type %in% c("Morning Commute", "Evening Commute"), "Commute","Non-Commute")) %>%
  group_by(timestamp, day_type, time_of_day, commute_period) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

hourly_ridership
```

Commute vs. Non-commute time periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Commute"])
```

```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
```

Weekday vs. Weekend periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekday"])
```

```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"])
qqline(hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$day_type == "Weekend"])
```

Assumptions check for t-tests:

- Commute vs. Non-commute time
  - We do not know the population SD (we took a sample of a typical week with no holidays or off season periods)
  - Sample size is large enough (per the CLT) for the test to be robust against normality violations
  - Independent observation assumption may be violated due to time data, but continue with t-test for this class

- Weekday vs. Weekend
  - We do not know the population SD (we took a sample of a typical week with no holidays or off season periods)
  - Sample size is large enough (per the CLT) for the test to be robust against normality violations
  - Independent observation assumption may be violated due to time data, but continue with t-test for this class
  
```{r}
# t-test for commute time vs. non-commute time means
commute_period_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ commute_period, data = hourly_ridership)
commute_period_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of commute periods = Mean hourly ridership of non-commute periods

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of commute periods ≠ Mean hourly ridership of non-commute periods

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = 1.975e-130 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly ridership during commute periods is different that the mean hourly ridership during non-commute

```{r}
# t-test for weekday vs. weekend means
weekday_weekend_test <- t.test(total_ridership ~ day_type, data = hourly_ridership)
weekday_weekend_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of Weekdays = Mean hourly ridership of weekends

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of Weekdays ≠ Mean hourly ridership of weekends

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = 7.411e-06 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is different that the mean hourly ridership of weekends

**ANOVA: Differences in mean hourly ridership between time-of-day categories**

ANOVA Assumptions Check:
```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (time_category in unique(hourly_ridership$time_of_day)) {
  x <- hourly_ridership$total_ridership[hourly_ridership$time_of_day == time_category]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", time_category))
  qqline(x)
}
```

```{r}
leveneTest(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)
```

- Normality, homogeneity of variances, independence of errors
  - All three assumptions may be violated based on the checks conducted.
    - QQ plots show deviation from normality, but sample sizes are large enough for test to be robust
    - Levene's test shows heteroscedasticity
    - Our sample was specifically selected not at random
  - This may be a limitation of this ANOVA analysis

```{r}
time_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ time_of_day, data = hourly_ridership)
summary(time_anova)
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership during morning = Mean hourly ridership during midday = Mean hourly ridership during evening = Mean hourly ridership during night

Alternative hypothesis: The mean hourly ridership of at least one time of day category is different than the others.

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = <2e-16 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that at least one time category group has a different mean hourly ridership than the others.

```{r}
time_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(time_anova)
time_post_hoc
```

Post hoc conclusions:
- At the alpha = 0.05 level, the time periods pairings that have a significant difference are:
  - Midday and Evening
  - Morning and Evening
  - Night and evening
  - Night and midday
  - Night and morning
- Out of these, I think the notable differences in pairs are midday and evening and morning and evening (it makes sense that night is significantly lower than the others).

**ANOVA: Differences in daily ridership between boroughs**
```{r}
# Daily ridership total for each borough
borough_daily <- project %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  group_by(date, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

ANOVA Assumptions Check:
```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

for (b in unique(borough_daily$borough)) {
  x <- borough_daily$total_ridership[borough_daily$borough == b]
  qqnorm(x, main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", b))
  qqline(x)
}
```

```{r}
leveneTest(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)
```
- Normality, homogeneity of variances, independence of errors
  - Normality and independence of errors have concern for violation
    - QQ plots show deviation from normality in each borough, the sample sizes for each borough are also relatively low
    - Our sample was specifically selected not at random
  - Homogeneity of variance may also be violated, but there is evidence for homogeneity of variances at the alpha = 0.1 level
  - Given these findings, this may be a limitation of this ANOVA analysis

```{r}
# Daily ridership total for each borough
borough_daily <- project %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(timestamp)) %>%
  group_by(date, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_ridership = sum(ridership, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
# ANOVA test: Do daily averages in each borough differ?
borough_anova <- aov(total_ridership ~ borough, data = borough_daily)
summary(borough_anova)
```

Null hypothesis: Mean daily ridership in Manhattan = Mean daily ridership in Brooklyn = Mean daily ridership in Queens = Mean daily ridership in the Bronx

Alternative hypothesis: The mean daily ridership of at least one borough is different than the others.

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = 1.38e-11 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that at least one borough has a different mean daily ridership than the other boroughs.

```{r}
borough_post_hoc <- TukeyHSD(borough_anova)
borough_post_hoc
```

Post hoc conclusions:
- At the alpha = 0.05 level, the borough pairings that have a significant difference are:
  - Brooklyn and the Bronx
  - Manhattan and the Bronx
  - Manhattan and Brooklyn
  - Queens and Manhattan
- Manhattan's mean daily ridership differs significantly from the mean daily ridership in all other boroughs

```{r, Boxplot-graph-daily-ridership-by-borough}

       aes(x = borough, y = total_ridership, fill = borough)) +

    "Bronx" = "#6B8E72",
    "Brooklyn" = "#008C7A",
    "Manhattan" = "#176B5B",
    "Queens" = "#42BFA5"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Ridership Distribution by Borough",
    x = "Borough",
    y = "Daily Total Ridership"
  ) +
  theme_mygraphs() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

#QQ Plots for Ridership by Borough
```{r}
hourly_transfers_total <- project %>%
  group_by(hour, borough) %>%
  summarize(total_hourly_transfers = sum(transfers, na.rm = TRUE),
  .groups = "drop"
)
boroughs <- unique(hourly_transfers_total$borough)
par(mfrow = c(2,2))

for (b in boroughs) {
  borough_data <- hourly_transfers_total$total_hourly_transfers[
    hourly_transfers_total$borough == b
  ]

  qqnorm(borough_data,
         main = paste("Q-Q Plot:", b),
         xlab = "Theoretical Quantiles",
         ylab = "Sample Quantiles")

  qqline(borough_data, col = "#72C47A", lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
All boroughs do not have a normal distribution of transfers. There are extreme points in the upper right quadrant in the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens, likely indicating an extremely low number of people taking the bus to the subway late in the evening. All boroughs show extreme values in the lower left quadrant, indicating few people take the bus to the subway during the early hours of the day. The step in the middle of the the graphs may indicate steep decrease following the morning commute followed by a more gradual decrease.
#Hypothesis Testing of Transfers
Questions of interest:

- Which hours have the highest transfers average (weekdays vs. weekends)? 

- Do these hours correspond to commuting periods? 
  
**T-Tests: Commute vs. Non-commute; Weekday vs. Weekend**
```{r}
hourly_transfers <- project %>%
  mutate(commute_period = if_else(commute_type %in% c("Morning Commute", "Evening Commute"), "Commute","Non-Commute")) %>%
  group_by(timestamp, day_type, time_of_day, commute_period) %>%
  summarize(total_transfers = sum(transfers, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

hourly_transfers
```

Commute vs. Non-commute time periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Commute"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Commute"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Non-Commute"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$commute_period == "Non-Commute"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

Weekday vs. Weekend periods:
```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekday"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekday"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
qqnorm(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekend"])
qqline(hourly_transfers$total_transfers[hourly_transfers$day_type == "Weekend"], col = "#B84A12", lwd = 2)
```

Assumptions check for t-tests:

- Commute vs. Non-commute time
  - Population SD unknown
  - Sample size is large enough (per the CLT) for the test to be robust against normality violations
  - Independent observation assumption may be violated due to time data, but continue with t-test for this class

- Weekday vs. Weekend
  - Population SD unknown
  - Sample size is large enough (per the CLT) for the test to be robust against normality violations
  - Independent observation assumption may be violated due to time data, but continue with t-test for this class
  
```{r}
# t-test for commute time vs. non-commute time means
commute_period_test <- t.test(total_transfers ~ commute_period, data = hourly_transfers)
commute_period_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of commute periods = Mean hourly ridership of non-commute periods

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of commute periods ≠ Mean hourly ridership of non-commute periods

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = 1e-08 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly transfers amounts during commute periods is different that the mean hourly transfers amounts during non-commute

```{r}
# t-test for weekday vs. weekend means
weekday_weekend_test <- t.test(total_transfers ~ day_type, data = hourly_transfers)
weekday_weekend_test
```

Null hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of Weekdays = Mean hourly ridership of weekends

Alternative hypothesis: Mean hourly ridership of Weekdays ≠ Mean hourly ridership of weekends

Alpha = 0.05 > P-value = 4e-06 --> Reject the null hypothesis. There is sufficient evidence to conclude that the mean hourly ridership on weekdays is different that the mean hourly ridership of weekends
